title: Put down the compiler: learn why non-buyers walk away before building more features
summary: Early-stage companies with a shaky v1.0 and downloads but few sales should stop coding and interview the people who left without buying. Cohen dismantles the common excuses (new feature, polish, I'm a user myself, it's marketing's job) and argues feedback from lost sales is the only real fix.

principles.text: When downloads or signups don't convert, the fix is feedback from lost sales, not your own theories about why people aren't buying.
principles.quote: This problem is solved only one way: **You need feedback from lost sales.**

principles.text: Prioritize talking to people who found you, read your copy, downloaded, then left silently; they are the low-hanging fruit who should be buying today.
principles.quote: You need to talk with the people who were interested enough to find your website, read your marketing copy, download your product, and then *give up without even an email*.

principles.text: Existing customers can't reveal sales barriers because they bought despite them; learn about conversion from the 98% who didn't buy.
principles.quote: Existing customers bought *in spite of* barriers to sale, so they're no help in identifying the barriers.

principles.text: 'One more feature' is almost never what blocks sales; the real blocker is often mundane, like a blank first screen or a broken installer.
principles.quote: Often the real impediment to sales is as mundane as "New users are presented with a blank screen, so they don't know what to do next, so they abandon the trial,"

principles.text: Being a user of your own product makes you the worst judge of the new-user experience; you are not your typical user.
principles.quote: Most of your users are dumb; almost all are dumber than you are. You are not your typical user.

principles.text: In a startup, getting revenue is everyone's job. If you don't know why people aren't buying, that is the #1 bug and #1 feature to work on.
principles.quote: In a startup, it's *everyone's* job to get revenue.
